# Faithfully

Marcus Hale had lived inside the sound of the sea for so long that silence, when it came, frightened him more than any storm.

He'd taken the position at Gull Point in the autumn of 1987, young enough to find the isolation romantic, old enough to know the romance would wear through like the elbows of a good coat. He and Eleanor had driven up the coast in a borrowed truck, their furniture roped in the bed, Eleanor holding a coffee can of marigold seeds in her lap because she said she refused to live anywhere without color. She'd planted them along the south wall of the keeper's cottage that first October, and they'd bloomed every summer since — even this summer, four years after she was gone.

He still didn't know how they kept coming back without her.

The lighthouse itself was a modest tower, sixty-two feet of whitewashed granite jutting from the headland like a raised finger. The light had been automated since 1994, which meant Marcus's official duties had shrunk considerably: he maintained the equipment, kept the logbook, watched the weather instruments, and filed monthly reports to the Coast Guard station in Harwick. In practice, what he did was watch. He watched the water change color through the seasons — pewter in winter, hammered gold in July, a particular shade of bruised purple in late October that he'd never seen matched anywhere else on earth. He watched the birds. He watched the ships.

He watched, and he kept the logbook, and he waited for something he couldn't name.

His daughter, Patricia, called every Sunday from Portland. "Dad, there are condos," she would say, which was her shorthand for a longer argument about his age, his isolation, his diet, the fact that the nearest hospital was forty minutes away on roads that iced badly in winter. "Nice ones. They have a pool." Marcus would make a sound that wasn't quite agreement and wasn't quite dismissal, and Patricia would sigh the sigh she had inherited directly from her mother.

---

The storm came on a Thursday in late October, the twenty-third. Marcus had been watching the barometer drop for two days. He'd radioed Harwick on Wednesday evening and the duty officer, a young woman named Connelly who had a competent, unhurried voice, confirmed what the instruments already told him: a nor'easter, possibly severe, landfall expected overnight into Thursday. She asked if he needed anything. He said no. She said to stay inside and he said he would, which was the kind of promise you made without any particular intention of keeping.

By four in the afternoon the sky had taken on that peculiar greenish light that precedes serious weather, and the sea had begun to organize itself into long, purposeful swells. Marcus ate an early supper — soup from a can, bread he'd baked on Tuesday, a glass of rye whiskey that Eleanor would have called unnecessary and he called essential — and then climbed the tower to check the light.

The light was running fine, as it always ran fine. The automated mechanism was reliable in a way that Marcus found both reassuring and vaguely insulting. He stood in the lantern room and looked out at the water and felt the first shudders of wind move through the tower's bones. Sixty-two feet of granite, and still the wind found ways to make it tremble.

He stayed up there longer than he needed to, watching the storm approach from the northeast. It came like a wall — not a metaphor but a literal wall, a hard vertical line where the sky darkened absolutely. He watched it move across the water toward him and felt, as he sometimes did in moments of great natural force, something he could only describe as gratitude. Not happiness, not peace, but gratitude — the specific gratitude of a person who has been given something enormous to witness.

Eleanor had felt it too. That was part of why they'd stayed.

---

The storm hit at nine-seventeen. Marcus had the time precisely because he'd just noted it in the logbook when the first serious gust came through — a sound like a freight train taking a corner too fast — and then the rain arrived and there was no more sound at all, only percussion.
